summary: Defines a MIB module extending the Interfaces Group MIB with common objects for managing multi-pair bonded xDSL interfaces, as defined in ITU-T Recommendations G.998.1, G.998.2, and G.998.3. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes several phone wires are tied together to carry data faster. This memo defines a standard set of dials for checking and controlling such a bundle.

questions: managing bonded dsl interfaces with snmp
how many lines can be bonded in g.bond
what is a gbs and bce in g.bond
subtitle: A common SNMP MIB module for managing xDSL lines bonded together into one logical link.

tldr.problem: Service providers bond several xDSL lines into one faster, more resilient link under ITU-T G.998.1, G.998.2 and G.998.3, but they need a common way to manage the bonded interface through SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The GBOND-MIB module extends the Interfaces Group MIB with objects for configuration, capabilities, status, discovery and performance monitoring that are shared by all three bonding schemes. A separate IANA-maintained module lists the schemes.
tldr.outcome: A bonded port shows up as an ordinary interface that stacks over up to 32 line or channel interfaces, and scheme-specific details live in three companion MIB modules.

today: RFC 6765 is a Proposed Standard and the data shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is used together with the scheme-specific modules in RFC 6766, RFC 6767 and RFC 6768.

sections.title: What G.Bond Is
sections.content:
xDSL multi-pair bonding lets a provider deliver high-bandwidth service over several xDSL lines, with more speed and resiliency than one line. The three schemes, collectively called G.Bond, are ATM-based bonding (G.998.1), Ethernet-based bonding (G.998.2) and bonding with Time-Division Inverse Multiplexing, or TDIM (G.998.3).

Each defines a new bonded sub-layer stacked above several per-line or per-bearer-channel sub-layers. All schemes allow bonding of up to 32 line or channel sub-layers with variable rates. Bonding several bearer channels of the same xDSL line is not allowed.

RFC 6765 defines the MIB module common to all three schemes. Scheme-specific objects are in the G9981-MIB (RFC 6768), G9982-MIB (RFC 6767) and G9983-MIB (RFC 6766). The textual conventions listing the schemes are in a separate IANA-maintained module, so new schemes can be added without reissuing the common module.
sections.plainLanguage: If one thin pipe is too slow, you can join several pipes side by side so water flows faster. This document is about the control panel for such a bundle of pipes.

sections.title: Layering and the Interfaces Group MIB
sections.content:
A bonded port is a stacked interface, so it is managed with the generic objects of the IF-MIB (RFC 2863). The RFC calls the bonded interface the Generic Bonding Sub-layer (GBS) and each underlying line or channel the Bonding Channel Entity (BCE). A GBS can aggregate up to 32 BCEs.

Each GBS and each BCE is its own row in the ifTable, and each must have a unique ifIndex. The GBS has an ifType of g9981(263), g9982(264) or g9983(265); a BCE uses the type of its xDSL technology, such as shdsl(169) or vdsl(97).

The ifStackTable records which BCEs are connected to which GBS, and its inverse ifInvStackTable (RFC 2864) answers the opposite question. The ifCapStackTable and ifInvCapStackTable from the IF-CAP-STACK-MIB (RFC 5066) describe which connections are possible. Because a BCE may also be limited by a GBS's capacity or already be in use, a manager must check these tables together with gBondPortCapCapacity.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a big hose (the bonded link) made from several small hoses. Each hose, big and small, gets its own name tag so it can be checked on its own.

sections.title: Bonding, Discovery and Initialization
sections.content:
Bonding splits incoming traffic into several streams, sends each over its own BCE and recombines them at the remote GBS, preserving the original order. For G.998.2, ports with several BCEs must fragment and reassemble Ethernet frames. For a single-BCE port this may be omitted, called bonding bypass, to avoid overhead and to interoperate with non-G.998 equipment. The agent is required to indicate every bonding scheme it supports. Setting the admin scheme objects to anything other than none turns on fragmentation and reassembly, even on a single-BCE port.

Ports may optionally support discovery: during initialization BCEs exchange information about their aggregation groups over the G.994.1 handshake. This can detect copper misconnections or automatically assign BCEs to groups. Each GBS gets a unique 6-octet discovery code, and writing it to a remote register is an atomic Set-if-Clear action that succeeds only if the register was zero. The RFC gives pseudocode for this as an example, noting implementations may instead use fixed or manual assignment.

Initialization, or training, can take tens of seconds. Setting ifAdminStatus to up on a GBS initializes all its BCEs. The GBS is operationally up if at least one BCE is up, lowerLayerDown if all are down, and notPresent if it has no BCE. During initialization it stays down and gBondPortStatFltStatus shows init. The RFC recommends rejecting, with inconsistentValue, removal of the last operationally up BCE from an up GBS, since that would drop the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the wires work together they need to find out which ones belong to the same team and warm up. The control panel lets you start that and see how it is going.

sections.title: Structure of the GBOND-MIB Module
sections.content:
The module follows the layout recommended by RFC 4181 and is split into two groups. gBondPort holds objects for configuration, capabilities, status, historical performance monitoring and notifications for each GBS. gBondBce holds a single object, the remote discovery code per BCE; the rest of the BCE objects live in the xDSL line MIB modules and in the scheme-specific modules.

The port group has configuration, capability and status tables. Examples are the desired scheme (gBondPortConfAdminScheme), the 6-octet gBondPortConfDiscoveryCode, the capacity of the local and peer GBS (1 to 32 BCEs), the bonding schemes supported as a bitmap, and the number of BCEs currently aggregated (0 to 32). Changing the admin scheme or discovery code must be done while the link is administratively down, otherwise it is rejected with inconsistentValue.

Section 5.3 maps Broadband Forum TR-159 managed objects to MIB objects, for example aGroupCapacity to gBondPortCapCapacity and aGroupOperState to ifOperStatus. The module is registered under mib-2 as node 211.
sections.plainLanguage: The control panel has a few groups of dials: some to set things, some that show what the bundle can do, and some that show what it is doing right now.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring
sections.content:
The optional Performance Monitoring counters, thresholds and history buckets from TR-159 use the 64-bit textual conventions of the HC-PerfHist-TC-MIB (RFC 3705). They count events such as errored seconds (ES), severely errored seconds (SES) and unavailable seconds (UAS) over 15-minute and one-day intervals. The exact definition of ES and SES can depend on the bonding scheme and is left to the scheme-specific module.

The agent SHOULD align each interval to a quarter-hour boundary of the wall clock and each one-day interval to the start of a day, so a management system can timestamp intervals from many agents. Counters are not reset when a GBS is re-initialized, only when the agent is reset or re-initialized. Some counters stop while service is unavailable, as each object's description says.
sections.plainLanguage: The bundle keeps a diary of how many bad moments it had in every quarter hour and every day, so someone can look back and see how healthy it was.

sections.title: The IANA-Maintained Scheme Module
sections.content:
The IANA-GBOND-TC-MIB module defines two textual conventions: IANAgBondScheme, an integer naming one scheme, and IANAgBondSchemeList, a bitmap of schemes. The values are none(0), g9981(1), g9982(2) and g9983(3). The value none means no bonding, an unknown value, or a single-BCE G.998.2 port using bonding bypass.

When a new bonding scheme appears in a revision of G.998, IANA can add it to this module, and any scheme-specific meaning of an existing object is described in the matching G998x-MIB, so GBOND-MIB need not be reissued. An Expert Review is required for each addition. The module is registered under mib-2 as node 215.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of bonding styles is kept in a separate notebook, so a new style can be written in without redoing the whole control panel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects can hurt the network if SET operations are not protected. The RFC lists examples: changing the admin scheme can lock the link if the peer does not support it; changing the discovery code before discovery can cause wrongful discovery; changing target data rates can degrade or fail the link; activating a line can cause cross-talk that degrades another port; and removing a channel from an up port can lower its data rate.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. Because bonded pairs are voice-grade copper that may share a bundle with pairs of another operator or customer, it is theoretically possible to eavesdrop by listening to cross-talk, especially if the link's parameters are known. The gBondPortStatTable is singled out for this reason.

Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. It is the operator's job to give access only to principals who have legitimate rights.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the wires sit close to other people's wires, the settings and readings are private. Only trusted people should be allowed to look at or change them.
